legend: Aki is fond of numbers, especially those with trailing zeros. For example, the number 9200%%ZSMJ0%% has two trailing zeros. Aki thinks the more trailing zero digits a number has, the prettier it is.

However, Aki believes, that the number of trailing zeros of a number is not static, but depends on the base (radix) it is represented in. Thus, he considers a few scenarios with some numbers and bases. And now, since the numbers he used become quite bizarre, he asks you to help him to calculate the beauty of these numbers.

Given two integers n%%ZSMJ1%% and b%%ZSMJ2%% (in decimal notation), your task is to calculate the number of trailing zero digits in the b%%ZSMJ3%%-ary (in the base/radix of b%%ZSMJ4%%) representation of n!%%ZSMJ5%% (factorial of n%%ZSMJ6%%).
input: The only line of the input contains two integers n%%ZSMJ7%% and b%%ZSMJ8%% (1≤n≤1018%%ZSMJ9%%, 2≤b≤1012%%ZSMJ10%%).
output: Print an only integer — the number of trailing zero digits in the b%%ZSMJ11%%-ary representation of n!%%ZSMJ12%%
note: In the third and fourth example, 5!(10)=120(10)=1111000(2)%%ZSMJ14%%.

The representation of the number x%%ZSMJ15%% in the b%%ZSMJ16%%-ary base is d1,d2,…,dk%%ZSMJ17%% if x=d1bk−1+d2bk−2+…+dkb0%%ZSMJ18%%, where di%%ZSMJ19%% are integers and 0≤di≤b−1%%ZSMJ20%%. For example, the number 720%%ZSMJ21%% from the first example is represented as 880(9)%%ZSMJ22%% since 720=8⋅92+8⋅9+0⋅1%%ZSMJ23%%.
You can read more about bases here.
